stem: A client with cancer-related fatigue says, "I think I should stay in bed all day so I do not waste any energy." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Plan short periods of rest, prioritize important activities for times when energy is better, and use a level of physical activity developed with the health care team.
options.B: Reduce activity to essential self-care and spend most of the remaining day resting until the fatigue resolves, then gradually return to the previous activity level.
options.C: Continue the usual daily schedule at the same pace despite fatigue so the body does not become accustomed to lower activity during cancer treatment.
options.D: Use rest as the main strategy during treatment and postpone an exercise plan until cancer therapy is completed, because activity can add to treatment-related fatigue.

rationale: Current National Cancer Institute guidance recommends planning time to rest, using short daytime naps when needed, prioritizing important activities, and scheduling them when energy is highest. NCI also states that exercise or physical activity can help people with cancer feel better and have more energy and recommends developing an appropriate activity plan with the health care team or physical therapist. Therefore A is correct. B makes inactivity the dominant strategy until fatigue disappears, C ignores pacing and symptom burden, and D unnecessarily postpones individualized physical activity until treatment is over.
educational_objective: Manage cancer-related fatigue with planned short rest and activity prioritization while maintaining individualized safe physical activity rather than relying on prolonged inactivity or pushing through fatigue.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health

source_claim_supported: Cancer-related fatigue management includes planned short rest, prioritization and timing of important activities, and individualized physical activity rather than routine prolonged inactivity.

supporting_sources.organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
supporting_sources.locator: Exercise: studies support a beneficial effect of exercise/physical activity on fatigue during and after cancer treatment; tailored approaches are needed because type, intensity, frequency, and rest intervals vary by client and treatment context.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Physical activity can reduce cancer-related fatigue and should be individualized rather than withheld routinely.

supporting_sources.organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
supporting_sources.document_title: Physical Activity and Cancer Fact Sheet
supporting_sources.locator: Is physical activity beneficial for cancer survivors?: strong evidence supports aerobic and/or resistance exercise during and after cancer treatment to reduce fatigue and improve physical function.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Appropriate physical activity is beneficial for fatigue and function in people with cancer.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort, printed pp. 36–37 (PDF pp. 39–40): Mobility/Immobility — implement measures to promote mobilization and evaluate client response; Rest and Sleep — assess the client's sleep/rest pattern and intervene as needed and schedule client care activities to promote adequate rest; Nonpharmacological Comfort Interventions — plan and provide comfort interventions for impaired comfort.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — activity/rest balance and energy conservation for cancer-related fatigue
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four responses to eliminate the uniquely-long keyed answer and replace simplistic inactivity distractors with realistic errors in pacing and activity planning. The corrected item directly tests balanced rest, prioritization, and individualized activity using current NCI guidance.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Cancer-related fatigue — activity/rest balance and energy conservation
audit_findings.stem: PASS — presents a common fatigue-management misconception and asks for one corrective nursing response.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly combines NCI-supported planned rest, prioritization/timing of important activities, and individualized activity; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — rest and essential self-care may be appropriate on difficult days, but making prolonged inactivity the default until fatigue resolves conflicts with guidance supporting individualized activity during treatment.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — maintaining function is desirable, but ignoring fatigue and continuing the same pace conflicts with pacing and prioritization strategies.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — rest has a role, but NCI supports exercise/physical activity during as well as after treatment rather than routine postponement until therapy ends.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only response that balances rest with safe ongoing activity and adapts the plan to the client's fatigue and treatment context.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B overemphasizes inactivity, C ignores fatigue, and D delays a supported intervention without clinical justification.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — alternatives are comparable in length and clinical detail and the keyed response is not uniquely long.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes mobilization, rest/sleep assessment and intervention, and comfort measures.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether B could be reasonable energy conservation; NCI explicitly pairs short planned rest and prioritization with individualized exercise/physical activity, so prolonged inactivity until fatigue resolves is not the best general plan and A remains uniquely correct.
